notes.text: or [So Israel and his family started traveling toward Egypt with all his belongings]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. or [burned some of his animals on an altar there as sacrifices]
Consider again how you translated the idiom **Behold me** throughout the book of Genesis. See 22:1, 7, 11; 27:1, 18; 31:11; 37:13; 46:2. or [Yes, Master?] or [I am listening, Lord]
or [to go to the country of Egypt and settle there]
This clause refers to the custom of closing a person’s eyes after he died and means that Joseph would be with Jacob when he died.
For a note about how **Pharaoh** is used like a name in the Bible, see 12:15. or [that the king of Egypt]

The pronoun **him** refers to Jacob, the head of his family, and includes Jacob’s wives and children. It may be necessary to use the plural pronoun “them” to make that clear. or [for them to ride on to Egypt]

For some languages, it may be clearer or more natural to change the order of the clauses in this verse and say, “He/Jacob brought his entire extended family with him to Egypt, including his sons …” or [Jacob had all his descendants with him when he arrived in Egypt]

Numbers 26:24 and 1 Chronicles 7:1 have the same list of Issachar’s sons as here, but instead of **Puvah** and “Job,” they have “Puah” and “Jashub.” Some translations keep the spelling for these names the same in all three locations to avoid confusion.
Be consistent with how you spell the name **Dinah** in the book of Genesis. See 30:21; 34:1–5, 11, 13, 25–26; 46:15. or [in addition to their daughter Dinah]
or [who were his blood relatives] or [who were his biological descendants]

For some languages it is clearer and more natural to change the order of the clauses in this sentence and say, “Altogether Jacob had sixty-six blood relatives who went with him to Egypt. That number does not include his wives or his sons’ wives.”
or [When they reached Egypt, he had Judah go]

Goshen was a region or territory that was part of the country of Egypt. For some languages it is better to make that explicit here, rather than wait until the end of the verse. Also be consistent here with how you spelled **Goshen** in Genesis 45:10. or [to Goshen County]
Make sure that the way Joseph refers to Pharaoh here sounds respectful in your translation. See what you did in Genesis 41:35.

notes.quote: אַנְשֵׁ֨י מִקְנֶ֜ה הָי֤וּ עֲבָדֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ מִ⁠נְּעוּרֵ֣י⁠נוּ וְ⁠עַד־עַ֔תָּה
notes.text: The phrase “Your servants” shows respect to Pharaoh and acknowledges his high position. It does not mean that Pharaoh actually owns Joseph’s brothers as servants. Translate this in a polite way that shows respect toward Pharaoh.
The idea here is that Jacob’s family would be permitted to live in rural areas to raise their livestock away from most Egyptians, who despised sheep herders. or [he will permit you to live privately]

For some languages it is clearer and more natural to change the order of phrases in this clause. or [the people of Egypt have disdain for sheep herders] or [Egyptians detest everyone who raises sheep]
